questions.q: What does the `@dataclass` decorator automatically generate for a class?
options: A database table matching the class's fields
`__init__`, a readable `__repr__`, and `__eq__`, based on the class's annotated fields
A REST API endpoint for the class
Automatic multithreading support
questions.explain: @dataclass inspects the class's type-annotated fields and writes the common boilerplate methods for you, so you don't hand-write them.

questions.q: In `@dataclass class APIConfig: api_key: str; base_url: str = "https://api.example.com"`, which field(s) are required when creating an instance?
options: Both fields are required
Neither field is required
Only `base_url`, because it has a default
Only `api_key`, because it has no default value
questions.explain: A field without a default must be supplied when constructing the instance; a field with a default value becomes optional.

questions.q: How does equality (`==`) behave differently for two instances of the same dataclass with identical field values, compared to two instances of an equivalent plain class?
options: A dataclass's `==` compares field values (so they're equal); a plain class's default `==` compares object identity (so they're not equal, even with the same values)
There is no difference between the two
A plain class's `==` always raises an error
A dataclass's `==` always returns False regardless of field values
questions.explain: @dataclass generates __eq__ that compares the declared fields' values. A plain class without a custom __eq__ falls back to identity comparison, so two separately created instances with the same data would NOT be equal.

options: Prevents the class from being subclassed
Makes every field default to `None`
Makes instances immutable — attempting to reassign a field after construction raises an error
Converts the dataclass into a dictionary automatically
questions.explain: frozen=True raises a FrozenInstanceError on any attempt to assign to a field after the object is created, which is useful for values that should never change once set.

questions.q: When is a dataclass a better fit than a regular hand-written class?
options: Only when the class needs no attributes at all
When the class's main job is holding structured data, with little custom behavior beyond init/repr/equality
Only for classes that will never be instantiated
Dataclasses always replace regular classes; there's no situation to prefer a regular class
questions.explain: Dataclasses shine for data-holding classes (configs, parsed responses, records). A class with significant custom behavior beyond the boilerplate dataclass generates is often still better as a regular class.
